implementation_notes: Scala's replacement for the classic structure is the contextual parameter: a RequestContext case class is built at the boundary and declared as an implicit (Scala 2) or given (Scala 3) value, so every method that declares (using ctx: RequestContext) receives it without an explicit argument - checked at compile time, with zero runtime lookup. Compared with a thread-local this keeps the dependency visible in the signature and testable by supplying a context directly; where only one layer needs the value, an ordinary parameter is still simpler.
pitfalls: An unbounded implicit chain hides which values are actually woven through the flow: ambiguity and missing-given errors surface far from the boundary that should have provided them.
Contextual parameters are resolved statically, so a value cannot be rebound mid-flow the way a thread-local can - an inner given shadows rather than mutates.

variants.name: IOLocal / FiberRef fiber-local state
variants.idiom_name: cats-effect IOLocal (ZIO FiberRef) for per-request values
variants.implementation_notes: Effect systems provide the ambient form: cats-effect's IOLocal is a fiber-local reference created with IOLocal(initial) and read/rebound with get/set/update inside IO, with the value inherited by child fibers at fork time and never shared back to the parent; ZIO's FiberRef is the same mechanism. It is the closest Scala analogue of a request-scoped thread-local, but only inside one effect runtime, and inheritance requires runtime bookkeeping (cats-effect needs cats.effect.trackFiberContext=true for propagation).
variants.code_sketch:
val requestCtx: IO[IOLocal[RequestContext]] = IOLocal(RequestContext.unknown)

def handle: IO[Receipt] =
  for
    ctx  <- requestCtx
    _    <- ctx.set(RequestContext(req.id, tenantOf(req)))   // bind for this fiber
    rc   <- ctx.get
    out  <- repo.save(rc.tenantId)
  yield out
pitfalls: Values are inherited at fork time: a fiber that outlives the request keeps the old value and never sees later updates made by the parent.
The reference only exists inside the effect runtime - work handed to a raw thread or executor outside IO loses the value entirely.
